Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

Take your kitten to a vet as soon as you can. Ask where you got her about any vaccines, deworming and food she has had.

- Vet visits: kittens usually see the vet every 3 to 4 weeks until about 6 months old, for shots and parasite treatment.
- Vaccines: the core kitten shots start at about 6 to 8 weeks and are repeated every 3 to 4 weeks until 16 to 20 weeks old.
- Deworming: worms are very common in kittens, so many vets deworm them routinely.
- Testing: a kitten with an unknown history should be tested for FeLV and FIV. Keep her apart from your other cats until the vet has checked her.
- Feeding: use kitten food, given several times a day.
- Litter box: one per cat, plus one extra, kept clean.

Chocolate is poisonous to dogs, especially dark and baking chocolate. Call or go to a vet now, even if your dog seems fine, because signs can take hours to show.

While you get there:
- Note the type of chocolate, how much, and when it was eaten
- Bring the wrapper if you can
- Don't make your dog vomit unless the vet tells you to

Watch for vomiting, restlessness, fast breathing, shaking or seizures, and tell the vet straightaway if you see them.

It could be. Common flea signs include:
- Scratching, biting or licking the skin a lot
- Hair loss or red skin near the tail and between or behind the legs
- Small red bumps or flaky skin
- Seeing adult fleas or "flea dirt" (tiny black specks of flea poop) in the fur

Some pets are allergic to flea bites, which makes the itching worse. A heavy flea load can cause blood loss (anemia). Fleas also spread tapeworms.

Itching can have other causes too, like mites or allergies, so have your vet check your dog. Ask your vet for a flea product that suits your dog's weight and age.

This sounds like it could be heatstroke. Overheating can damage organs within minutes. Flat-faced and thick-coated breeds are most at risk.

What to do now:
- Move them out of the sun right away, into shade or an air-conditioned room.
- Wet the coat with cool tap water, especially the belly, armpits, groin and paws, then fan them so the water evaporates.
- Offer small sips of cool water if they're alert. Don't force them to drink.
- Keep cooling for 10–15 minutes, then go to the vet with the car's air-con on, even if they seem better. Damage can show up hours later.
- If you have a rectal thermometer, stop active cooling at about 39.5 °C so they don't get too cold.

Don't:
- Ice or ice-cold water. It narrows blood vessels and slows cooling.
- Leaving a wet towel draped over them. It traps heat.
- Wet the coat and keep air moving instead. It doesn't cool them down.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Cats handle heat better than many dogs, but hot, humid days can still be dangerous.
- Keep fresh water in several places, and add wet food for extra fluids
- Give them a shaded, airy spot, and use a fan or air-con in the hottest hours
- Brush long-haired cats often to remove loose fur
- Never leave a cat in a parked car

Open-mouth panting, drooling, wobbliness or collapse can mean heatstroke. Move them somewhere cool and go to a vet now.

I haven't found any definitive information about when a nursing mother should be spayed, but spaying nursing mothers seems common in TNR (trap neuter return) groups (it's better to spay a cat that you have in a trap now, then try to trap her or your kitten back).

Ally Cat Allies (a leading TNR group) states:

"Nursing mother cats continue to produce milk after being spayed, and can continue to nurse their kittens until they are at least 3 months old."

So it sounds like you could probably wait until after your cat has finished nursing.

Adult dogs: most do well on 1 or 2 meals a day. The ASPCA suggests two meals, about 8 to 12 hours apart.

Adult cats (from about 1 year old): once or twice a day suits most cats. Leaving food out all day works for some cats, but makes others overeat and gain weight. Replace any food left out with fresh food daily.

How much:
- The amount on the label is based on an average pet. A less active pet may need less.
- Check your pet's body. You should be able to feel the ribs without pressing hard, and see a waist behind the ribs from above.
- If you can't feel the ribs without pressing, there is too much fat. Ask your vet how much to cut back.

Always keep fresh, clean water out.

Dogs:
- Trim when the nails touch the ground or click on the floor. For many dogs this is about monthly.
- Cut small bits at a time. On light nails, stop a little short of the pink quick. On dark nails, trim just the very tip.
- Don't forget the dewclaws.

Cats:
- Gently press the toe pad so the claw comes out.
- Snip only the sharp white tip. Avoid the pink part, which has nerves and blood vessels.
- Trim every 2 to 3 weeks. At first, do just one or two claws per session.

If a nail bleeds, press styptic powder or cornstarch on the tip and make sure it stops. If your pet fights or gets upset, stop. Your vet can help.

"Tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffening or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

Mouthing is normal for puppies. The goal is to teach them to be gentle.

- When teeth press hard, give a high-pitched yelp and let your hand go limp. Praise your puppy when they stop.
- If that doesn't work, ignore them for 10 to 20 seconds or walk away, then play again calmly.
- Keep a chew toy or tug toy handy and offer it when they go for your hands or feet.
- Play fetch or tug instead of rough games with your hands.
- Don't jerk your hands away. It invites more grabbing.
- Never hit, slap or shake your puppy. It can make biting worse and cause fear.

Get help from a certified animal behaviorist or veterinary behaviorist if bites come with a stiff body, growling or pulled-back lips, or hurt much more than play bites.

First, have your vet rule out a medical problem. Peeing outside the box can be a sign of a bladder problem.

Go to the vet now if your cat strains in the box with little or no pee coming out, cries while peeing, or is vomiting or very tired. A blocked bladder can kill, and male cats are most at risk.

If the vet finds nothing wrong, check the box:
- One box per cat, plus one extra
- Scoop daily, and change all the litter weekly
- Most cats like unscented, clumping, fine litter
- Put boxes in quiet spots, away from food bowls and busy areas

Stress, like a move or a new pet, can also cause it. Clean accidents with an enzyme cleaner for pet odors. Never punish your cat.

It is natural for a dog to have a light smell, I wouldn't bathe a dog unless it got dirty. Most dirt can simply be rubbed off the fur by using a dry towel, which I would prefer to bathing.

Dogs are waterproof, so as long as you are not using soap there isn't much to worry about. Our Labradors used to jump into every water source available, no matter how cold or smelly.

If you need to use soap, be sure to use a soap that is approved to be used on dogs. There are special soaps available in most pet stores or online that don't affect the protective layers on the skin too much.

No. Grapes and raisins can cause sudden kidney failure in dogs, and even a few can be dangerous for some dogs. There's no safe amount.

If your dog ate grapes or raisins:
- Go to a vet now, even if they seem fine
- Tell the vet how many and when

Safer treats include small pieces of plain cooked chicken, carrot or apple without the seeds.

Use a toothpaste made for pets. Never use human toothpaste. It isn't meant to be swallowed and can upset the stomach, and some contain xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

Steps:
- Start slowly. Rub a finger or soft cloth along the outside of a few teeth, near the gums.
- Let your pet lick a little pet toothpaste from your finger.
- Once they accept that, put toothpaste on the cloth, then move to a finger brush or small, soft toothbrush.
- Brush the outer surfaces at the gumline. Start with the big back teeth and the long fang teeth, where plaque builds up fastest. Aim for about 30 seconds per side.

Brush daily if you can, and at least three times a week. Keep sessions short and calm, and praise your pet.

Keep fresh, clean water out at all times, in places your pet can easily reach. Cats that eat wet food often drink less, because the food is mostly water. Cats on dry food need to drink more.

Signs of dehydration:
- Dry or sticky gums
- Skin that stays "tented" when you gently lift it at the back of the neck, instead of snapping back
- Sunken eyes, weakness, low energy or poor appetite

Vomiting and diarrhea can cause dehydration fast. Call your vet today if you think your pet is dehydrated. Go now if they haven't eaten or drunk anything for 24 hours, or are very weak.

Drinking much more than usual also needs a vet visit within a day. It can be a sign of kidney disease, diabetes or other illness.

Yes. The American Association of Feline Practitioners recommends core vaccines even for cats that never go outside. Core vaccines for cats cover:
- Panleukopenia (feline distemper)
- Herpesvirus
- Calicivirus
(these three come together as FVRCP)
- Rabies, where the disease is present or the law requires it

Feline leukemia (FeLV) vaccine is advised for kittens under 1 year. For adults it depends on risk, such as going outdoors or living with cats that do.

Good news for indoor cats: global guidelines say low-risk indoor adults usually need core boosters only every 3 years or longer.

Your vet will choose the vaccines and timing that fit your cat.

Parvovirus is a very contagious virus that attacks a dog's gut. Puppies and unvaccinated dogs are most at risk. It spreads through infected poop and anything it touches, and it can survive in the environment for months or longer.

Signs usually start 5 to 7 days after exposure:
- Dullness, fever and not eating
- Then vomiting and diarrhea, often bloody

Dogs lose fluids fast and can go into shock. Some die within hours, but most dogs that get hospital care survive. See a vet now if your puppy has vomiting or bloody diarrhea. Call ahead so the clinic can protect other patients.

Keep sick dogs away from others. Ask your vet how to disinfect your home, because many cleaners don't kill parvo.

Honestly, with cats it can be pretty hard to tell if they are in pain. It sounds to me like your cat is in pain. Here is a list of some (but by no means all) signs your cat is in pain:

- Cats don't typically groan or meow from ambient pain.
- Eating less than normal.
- Sleeping more than normal.
- Not interested in things that normally interest it, like play.
- Does not behave normally.
- Moving around looks more difficult.

They'll refrain from jumping, take stairs slowly, and so forth.

- Not to say they are incapable of moving quickly, as they may also be quick to swipe at you if some particular stimulus is present. For example, if they are scratching on a carpet, they could feel a little uncomfortable even though they aren't in pain. But they won't move until you stop stroking them.

Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them to keep practice until they feel comfortable, and clean the mess well.

Although your situation is for after a firework display, I think the best course of action that you can take is things you would typically do before and during a firework display as well.

At the minimum, I would bring the dog inside your home during the time of the fireworks (you said they tried to "jump the fence," I'm assuming that they are outside).

Usually, anxiety/thundershirts are recommended for these kind of situations as well.

The shirt helps to calm a dog due to the pressure being applied to them from the shirt. You can try a thudershirt both during and after a firework display.

I would say it would be pretty hard to train a dog to avoid a specific object. It takes practice to get used to it. But if you have patience and consistency, then it should work.

A basic kit helps in the first minutes, but it never replaces a vet. Useful items:
- Gauze, sterile pads, stretch bandage and adhesive tape
- Small blunt-tipped scissors and tweezers
- Saline solution for rinsing wounds and eyes
- Cotton balls or swabs and disposable gloves
- A muzzle for dogs, and a towel for wrapping or carrying
- A rectal thermometer and lubricating jelly
- Splint material
- A small supply of your pet's regular medicines
- Your vet's number, the nearest 24-hour clinic, and your pet's health records

Keep it in a box with a secure lid you can grab fast, and check expiry dates every year. Ask your vet before giving any medicine, and only make your pet vomit if a vet tells you to. In an emergency, go to your vet or nearest clinic now and use the kit on the way, then take your pet to the hospital as soon as possible.

Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats.

Ask your vet to score your pet and compare it to his/her age.

Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

Itching is a sign, not a disease. The three main causes are parasites (mainly fleas and mites, which are checked first), skin infections from bacteria, yeast or fungus, and allergies to things like insect bites, food, pollen, mold or dust. Itching only in certain seasons often points to a seasonal allergen.

Itching all year can point to dust mites or food.

What to check at home:
- Look through the coat for fleas or flea dirt, and at the skin for redness, scabs or hair loss
- Note where he scratches. Licking and rubbing of the feet and face is common with allergies and infections

See your vet if the itching lasts more than a few days, or if there is hair loss, scaling, a bad smell, or fluid on the skin.

Please don't give human allergy pills or leftover steroids.

Antihistamines often don't work on dogs.

If you think it's food allergies, ask your vet to test it.

One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

The best age depends on your pet, so ask your vet. General guidance:

Cats: Many groups advise spaying or neutering before about 5 months old. Some vets do it around 6 months. Healthy kittens can be fixed as young as 8 weeks.

Dogs: The traditional age is about 6 to 9 months, and some groups advise before 5 months. Giant-breed males kept as house pets are often neutered after they stop growing, at about 12 to 15 months.

Benefits include:
- No heat cycles and no unplanned litters
- Lower risk of womb infections and breast tumors in females
- No testicular cancer in males, and less roaming and urine marking

Pets can gain weight after surgery, so watch their food portions.

Please don't wait for signs. Raisins and grapes can cause kidney failure in dogs, so treat any amount seriously. Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now and take him in.

Vomiting or diarrhea often starts within 6 to 12 hours. Later signs include low energy, not eating, belly pain, weakness and drinking a lot. Kidney failure can develop within 1 to 3 days, and it is often fatal.

Before you go:
- Bring the bread or packaging so the vet can estimate how many raisins he ate.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

On the way, keep him calm and note any vomiting or diarrhea to tell the vet.

Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Normal shedding thins the coat evenly, with no bald patches. Hair loss is different: bald or thin patches, or hair missing from both sides of the body. Hair loss is a sign of another problem, not a disease on its own. Common causes in cats are fleas and flea allergy (the most common cause of hair loss on both sides), other parasites, fungal or bacterial skin infections, allergies, and overgrooming from stress or pain. See your vet if you notice: - Bald or thin patches, or red, scabby or sore skin - Your cat licking or scratching the same spot a lot - Hair loss that is sudden, spreading or not settling - Hair loss together with weight loss, low energy or a change in eating or drinking Your vet will check for fleas and skin infection, and may run skin, blood or urine tests to find the cause.

Ask your city or municipal veterinary office or barangay where and when they register dogs. Spayed or neutered dogs get a discounted registration fee under Section 10.

Humans' domestication of cats has caused them to retain many childhood actions and habits into adulthood and kneading (as in kneading bread) is thought to be one of them.

As you know, kittens knead at the mother's teats to cause lactation (the flow of milk). Can you imagine something better than being up close to Mom, all warm and cosy, getting delicious milk?

When an adult kneads, he or she is demonstrating an activity which was pleasurable for them in kittenhood and still gives them pleasure.

We have had kneaders that are so into it that I've often wondered if there is a way to get them help me knead the dough when I make bread.

If you are concerned about any urgent health issue with your pet, you should call a vet.

That having been said, cats are hunters and will eat small animals, including rodents, birds, insects, and lizards. If you don't notice anything unusual with your cat, there probably isn't anything to worry about. But again, if you are concerned, call your vet.

Every year. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must have their dogs "regularly" vaccinated against rabies. The implementing rules make it clearer: a properly immunized dog is one vaccinated yearly, and LGUs register and vaccinate dogs annually.

The shot must be given by a licensed veterinarian, or by a trained vaccinator under a vet's direct supervision during government mass vaccination drives.

Keep the record of each shot on your dog's vaccination or registration card.

Under Section 5 of RA 9482, the owner must:

- Report the bite to the concerned officials (for example your barangay or city/municipal veterinary or health office) within 24 hours
- Place the dog under observation by a government or private veterinarian
- Help the person who was bitten right away, and pay for their medical and related expenses

Tell the person to wash the wound and go to an Animal Bite Treatment Center promptly.

Refusing to have the dog observed carries a fine of P10,000, or P25,000 if you also refuse to pay the victim's medical costs (Section 11). Local amounts may differ, so check with your city or municipal veterinary office.

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.

Not in public. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must keep their dogs under control and not let them roam public places without a leash. LGUs must also make sure dogs are leashed or kept inside the owner's property (Section 7).

- The dog tag should be on the collar or harness
- Aggressive dogs should wear a muzzle in public

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now, even though he seems fine. Many rat poisons stop the blood from clotting, and bleeding may not show right away. Early treatment gives the best chance of recovery.

Signs to watch for:

- Bring the package or a photo of the label. Rat poisons work in different ways and need different treatment.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.

This can be a blocked bladder, which is an emergency in male cats. Take him to a vet now. A blockage can become life-threatening within a day.

Other signs include crying in the litter box, licking his genitals, vomiting, or hiding. Don't wait to see if it passes, and don't press on his belly. The vet can check his bladder and relieve the blockage.

This sounds like it could be bloat (twisted stomach). The stomach fills with gas and can twist. It can kill within hours and usually needs surgery. Most common in large, deep-chested dogs.

What to do now:
- Go to the vet immediately. Call ahead so they can prepare.
- Keep your dog as calm and still as you can on the way.

Don't:
- Waiting to see if it passes.
- Giving food, water or home remedies.
- Trying to make them vomit.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

This sounds like it could be snake bite. Venom spreads faster when your pet moves. Keep them still and get to a vet. Signs can be delayed.

What to do now:
- Keep yourself safe. Don't try to catch or kill the snake. Take a photo from a distance if it's easy.
- Keep your pet calm and still, and carry them if you can.
- Take off the collar if the bite is on the head or neck, because it may swell.
- Go to the vet now. Call ahead so they can check for antivenom.

Don't:
- Cutting the wound, sucking out venom, tourniquets or ice.
- Waiting for signs to appear.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Stay calm and focus on keeping him safe.

While it's happening:
- Move furniture and hard objects away. Only move him if he's near stairs, water or another danger.
- Keep your hands away from his mouth. He can't control his jaws and may bite without meaning to.
- Don't try to hold him down.
- Time the seizure, and take a short video for the vet if you can.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the seizure lasts more than about 3 minutes, if he has more than one in a row, or if he might have eaten something poisonous. Otherwise, call your vet soon after.

Afterward he may pace or seem confused. On the way to the vet, keep him calm, quiet and away from edges.

Yes. Please take him to a vet now, even if he looks fine. Some injuries don't show their full effects for a day or two, and pale gums, fast breathing or weakness can be signs of shock or internal bleeding.

To get him there safely:
- Be careful, because a hurt dog may bite. Use a cloth muzzle only if he is breathing normally and has no chest injury.
- If he can't walk well, slide him onto a firm, flat surface like a board or folded blanket, and keep his head, neck and back as still as possible.
- Keep him calm and quiet, and have someone else drive.

Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic as you leave so they're ready for him.

Remove ticks as soon as you find them:

This sounds like it could be heatstroke. Overheating can damage organs within minutes. Flat-faced and thick-coated breeds are most at risk.

What to do now:
- Move them out of the sun right away, into shade or an air-conditioned room.
- Wet the coat with cool tap water, especially the belly, armpits, groin and paws, then fan them so the water evaporates.
- Offer small sips of cool water if they're alert. Don't force them to drink.
- Keep cooling for 10–15 minutes, then go to the vet with the car's air-con on, even if they seem better. Damage can show up hours later.
- If you have a rectal thermometer, stop active cooling at about 39.5 °C so they don't get too cold.

Don't:
- Ice or ice-cold water. It narrows blood vessels and slows cooling.
- Leaving a wet towel draped over them.
- It traps heat.
- Wet the coat and keep air moving instead.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Cats handle heat better than many dogs, but hot, humid days can still be dangerous.
- Keep fresh water in several places, and add wet food for extra fluids
- Give them a shaded, airy spot, and use a fan or air-con in the hottest hours
- Brush long-haired cats often to remove loose fur
- Never leave a cat in a parked car

Open-mouth panting, drooling, wobbliness or collapse can mean heatstroke. Move them somewhere cool and go to a vet now.

- Panleukopenia (feline distemper)
- Herpesvirus

Feline leukemia (FeLV) vaccine is advised for kittens under 1 year. For adults it depends on risk, such as going outdoors or living with cats that do.

Your vet will choose the vaccines and timing that fit your cat.

Parvovirus is a very contagious virus that attacks a dog's gut. Puppies and unvaccinated dogs are most at risk. It spreads through infected poop and anything it touches, and it can survive in the environment for months or longer.

Signs usually start 5 to 7 days after exposure:
- Dullness, fever and not eating
- Then vomiting and diarrhea, often bloody

Dogs lose fluids fast and can go into shock. Some die within hours, but most dogs that get hospital care survive. See a vet now if your puppy has vomiting or bloody diarrhea. Call ahead so the clinic can protect other patients.

Keep sick dogs away from others. Ask your vet how to disinfect your home, because many cleaners don't kill parvo.

Honestly, with cats it can be pretty hard to tell if they are in pain. It sounds to me like your cat is in pain. Here is a list of some (but by no means all) signs your cat is in pain:

- Cats don't typically groan or meow from ambient pain.
- Eating less than normal.
- Sleeping more than normal.
- Not interested in things that normally interest it, like play.
- Does not behave normally.
- Moving around looks more difficult.

They'll refrain from jumping, take stairs slowly, and so forth.

- Not to say they are incapable of moving quickly, as they may also be quick to swipe at you if some particular stimulus is present. For example, if they are scratching on a carpet, they could feel a little uncomfortable even though they aren't in pain. But they won't move until you stop stroking them.

Patience, a routine and rewards work best.

- Take your puppy out at least every two hours, and right after waking up, eating and playing.
- Feed meals at the same times each day.
- Use the same outdoor spot each time, and say a cue word like "potty" while they go.
- Praise or give a treat right after they finish.
- Watch for sniffing, circling or scratching at the door, then go out right away.
- When you can't watch, use a crate or a small gated area.
- A puppy can often hold it about one hour per month of age. A 3-month-old may need a break about every 3 hours.

Never punish accidents. Calmly take the puppy to the outdoor spot, reward them to keep practice until they feel comfortable, and clean the mess well.

Although your situation is for after a firework display, I think the best course of action that you can take is things you would typically do before and during a firework display as well.

At the minimum, I would bring the dog inside your home during the time of the fireworks (you said they tried to "jump the fence," I'm assuming that they are outside).

Usually, anxiety/thundershirts are recommended for these kind of situations as well.

The shirt helps to calm a dog due to the pressure being applied to them from the shirt. You can try a thudershirt both during and after a firework display.

I would say it would be pretty hard to train a dog to avoid a specific object. It takes practice to get used to it. But if you have patience and consistency, then it should work.

A basic kit helps in the first minutes, but it never replaces a vet. Useful items:
- Gauze, sterile pads, stretch bandage and adhesive tape
- Small blunt-tipped scissors and tweezers
- Saline solution for rinsing wounds and eyes
- Cotton balls or swabs and disposable gloves
- A muzzle for dogs, and a towel for wrapping or carrying
- A rectal thermometer and lubricating jelly
- Splint material
- A small supply of your pet's regular medicines
- Your vet's number, the nearest 24-hour clinic, and your pet's health records

Keep it in a box with a secure lid you can grab fast, and check expiry dates every year. Ask your vet before giving any medicine, and only make your pet vomit if a vet tells you to. In an emergency, go to your vet or nearest clinic now and use the kit on the way, then take your pet to the hospital as soon as possible.

Dogs: The ASPCA suggests a bath at least once every three months. Dogs that spend a lot of time outdoors or have skin problems may need baths more often.

Cats: Most cats keep themselves clean. They only need a bath if they get very dirty or into something sticky or smelly.

Bath tips:
- Brush out loose hair and mats first.
- Use lukewarm water and a shampoo made for pets. Human shampoo can irritate or dry out the skin.
- Keep water out of the eyes, ears and nose. Wipe the face with a damp cloth.
- Rinse well and dry fully, including any skin folds.
- For cats, trim the claws first and use a rubber mat so they don't slip.

See your vet if you notice scabs, bald spots, redness or constant scratching.

Vets use a 9-point body condition score (BCS) from WSAVA. You can do a quick check at home:
- Ribs: Run your hands along the sides. At a healthy weight you can feel the ribs under a thin layer of fat. If you can't feel them without pressing, there is too much fat.
- Waist: Look down from above. You should see a waist behind the ribs.
- Belly: From the side, a dog's belly should tuck up. A cat at a healthy weight has only a small fat pad on the belly.

Signs of overweight are ribs that are hard to feel, no waist, a rounded belly, and fat over the lower back (and in dogs, the base of the tail).

Ideal is 4 to 5 out of 9 for dogs and 5 out of 9 for cats.

Ask your vet to score your pet and follow his/her advice.

Many cats bring up a hairball once every week or two, and that alone is usually not a worry. A hairball is a wet, tube-shaped wad of swallowed hair.

See your vet soon if she:
- Vomits more than once a week
- Seems tired or weak, or eats less
- Has blood in the vomit
- Drinks or pees more or less than usual, or also has diarrhea

Go now if she keeps retching or vomiting with nothing coming up, refuses food for more than a day, or is very weak. A hairball or a swallowed object like string can block the gut, and that can be fatal without surgery.

To help prevent hairballs, comb her coat daily, especially when she sheds. Don't give laxatives or hairball products unless your vet says so.

Book a vet visit soon. Your puppy will need a series of shots and deworming.

- Vaccines: puppies get shots every 2 to 3 weeks until they are about 4 months old. Your vet will set the exact schedule.
- Until the shots are done, keep your puppy away from dogs that may not be vaccinated.
- Deworming: worms are common in puppies. Your vet may deworm and check stool samples every 2 to 4 weeks until two tests in a row are clear.
- Feeding: puppies 6 to 12 weeks old usually eat 4 small meals a day of puppy food.
- Potty training: start early. Take the puppy out often and praise them when they go outside.
- Socializing: let them meet people and other animals gently, especially at 2 to 4 months old.

Most of the flea problem lives in your home, not on your pet. Eggs fall off into carpets, bedding and corners, and flea cocoons can wait there for months.

What helps:
- Treat every dog and cat in the home, not just the itchy one, using products your vet recommends
- Vacuum often
- Wash pet bedding and blankets regularly
- If you use a home spray, keep pets out of the room and follow the label
- Never put a house or yard product directly on a pet

Fleas can live indoors all year, so experts advise year-round flea prevention. It can take weeks to months of steady treatment to fully clear an infestation.

One vomit in a dog that otherwise seems well is often not serious, and many cases settle within a day. But vomiting can also be a sign of poisoning, a blockage or other illness.

Go to the vet right away if he vomits and also has:
- Blood in the vomit
- Diarrhea, belly pain or fever
- Low energy, no appetite or signs of dehydration
- A chance he swallowed something toxic or an object

See your vet today if vomiting goes on for more than 24 hours, even if he seems fine.

For a mild case, your vet may suggest resting the stomach for a short time, then small, frequent meals of a bland food. Keep fresh water available. Don't give human medicines unless your vet tells you to.

Mild diarrhea in an adult pet that is still bright and eating can sometimes be watched at home for a short time.

Home care:
- Always keep fresh water out. Diarrhea can quickly cause dehydration.
- Ask your vet about a short rest for the stomach, or small meals of a bland or gut-friendly diet.
- When the stool firms up, switch back to the usual food slowly over about a week.

See your vet if it lasts more than 24 hours.

Go now if there is:
- Blood in the stool, or black, tarry stool
- Vomiting, weakness, fever, belly pain or no appetite
- Diarrhea in a puppy. It can be an early sign of parvo, which can be deadly.
- Straining with nothing coming out

Normal shedding thins the coat evenly, with no bald patches. Hair loss is different: bald or thin patches, or hair missing from both sides of the body. Hair loss is a sign of another problem, not a disease on its own. Common causes in cats are fleas and flea allergy (the most common cause of hair loss on both sides), other parasites, fungal or bacterial skin infections, allergies, and overgrooming from stress or pain. See your vet if you notice: - Bald or thin patches, or red, scabby or sore skin - Your cat licking or scratching the same spot a lot - Hair loss that is sudden, spreading or not settling - Hair loss together with weight loss, low energy or a change in eating or drinking Your vet will check for fleas and skin infection, and may run skin, blood or urine tests to find the cause.

As you know, kittens knead at the mother's teats to cause lactation (the flow of milk). Can you imagine something better than being up close to Mom, all warm and cosy, getting delicious milk?

When an adult kneads, he or she is demonstrating an activity which was pleasurable for them in kittenhood and still gives them pleasure.

If you are concerned about any urgent health issue with your pet, you should call a vet.

That having been said, cats are hunters and will eat small animals, including rodents, birds, bugs, and lizards. If you don't notice anything unusual with your cat, there probably isn't anything to worry about. But again, if you are concerned, call your vet.

Every year. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must have their dogs "regularly" vaccinated against rabies. The implementing rules make it clearer: a properly immunized dog is one vaccinated yearly, and LGUs register and vaccinate dogs annually.

The shot must be given by a licensed veterinarian, or by a trained vaccinator under a vet's direct supervision during government mass vaccination drives.

Keep the record of each shot on your dog's vaccination or registration card.

Under Section 5 of RA 9482, the owner must:

- Report the bite to the concerned officials (for example your barangay or city/municipal veterinary or health office) within 24 hours
- Place the dog under observation by a government or private veterinarian
- Help the person who was bitten right away, and pay for their medical and related expenses

Tell the person to wash the wound and go to an Animal Bite Treatment Center promptly.

Refusing to have the dog observed carries a fine of P10,000, or P25,000 if you also refuse to pay the victim's medical costs (Section 11). Local amounts may differ, so check with your city or municipal veterinary office.

Under Section 9 of the Animal Welfare Act, as amended by RA 10631, sets penalties after conviction:

- Animal dies: 1 year, 6 months and 1 day to 2 years in prison, and/or a fine up to P100,000
- Animal survives but is severely injured and can't survive without human help: 1 year and 1 day to 1 year and 6 months, and/or up to P50,000
- Other cruelty or neglect: 6 months to 1 year, and/or up to P30,000

Penalties go up to 2 years and 1 day to 3 years and/or up to P250,000 if the offense involves a syndicate, a business, a public officer, or 3 or more animals.

Not in public. Section 5 of RA 9482 says owners must keep their dogs under control and not let them roam public places without a leash. LGUs must also make sure dogs are leashed or kept inside the owner's property (Section 7).

The implementing rules add:
- The leash should be no longer than 1.5 meters
- The dog tag should be on the collar or harness
- Aggressive dogs should wear a muzzle in public

The law sets a fine of P500 per incident for not leashing a dog outside the house (Section 11). These amounts are as written in the 2007 law. Your city or municipality may have its own ordinance, so check with your city or municipal veterinary office.

"Tick fever" usually means germs like Ehrlichia, Anaplasma or Babesia spread by ticks. In the Philippines, the warm climate suits the brown dog tick, which can live in homes and kennels. Ehrlichia canis was the most common tick-borne germ found in a study of dogs in Metro Manila and Laguna.

Signs may show 1 to 3 weeks after a bite:
- Fever, low energy, poor appetite
- Swollen glands, stiffening or limping
- Nosebleeds, bruises on the skin or gums, or blood in urine or poop

See a vet today if you notice bleeding, bruising, pale gums or weakness. A blood test is needed to confirm it.

Prevent it with year-round tick control your vet recommends and daily tick checks.

Often, yes. Section 6 of RA 9482 tells the Department of Agriculture to lead free anti-rabies vaccination of dogs, with priority for high-risk, low-income areas. LGUs must fund vaccines and run registration and vaccination (Section 7).

Executive Order No. 84 (1999) also calls for mass dog vaccination with free vaccines every March, Rabies Awareness Month.

Schedules differ by place, so watch for announcements from your barangay or ask your city or municipal veterinary office about the next free vaccination drive.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now, even though he seems fine. Many rat poisons stop the blood from clotting, and bleeding may not show right away. Early treatment gives the best chance of recovery.

Signs to watch for:
- Low energy, not eating, weakness, pale gums, fast breathing, nosebleeds, and blood in the urine, stool or eyes.

Before you go:
- Bring the package or a photo of the label. Rat poisons work in different ways and need different treatment.
- Only make him vomit if a vet tells you to.
- Check whether other pets could have eaten some.

On the way, handle him gently and keep him calm. Dogs and cats can also be poisoned by eating a poisoned rat, so tell the vet if that's possible.

This can be a blocked bladder, which is an emergency in male cats. Take him to a vet now. A blockage can become life-threatening within a day.

Other signs include crying in the litter box, licking his genitals, vomiting, or hiding. Don't wait to see if it passes, and don't press on his belly. The vet can check his bladder and relieve the blockage.

This sounds like it could be bloat (twisted stomach). The stomach fills with gas and can twist. It can kill within hours and usually needs surgery. Most common in large, deep-chested dogs.

What to do now:
- Go to the vet immediately. Call ahead so they can prepare.
- Keep your dog as calm and still as you can on the way.

Don't:
- Waiting to see if it passes.
- Giving food, water or home remedies.
- Trying to make them vomit.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

This sounds like it could be snake bite. Venom spreads faster when your pet moves. Keep them still and get to a vet. Signs can be delayed.

What to do now:
- Keep yourself safe. Don't try to catch or kill the snake. Take a photo from a distance if it's easy.
- Keep your pet calm and still, and carry them if you can.
- Take off the collar if the bite is on the head or neck, because it may swell.
- Go to the vet now. Call ahead so they can check for antivenom.

Don't:
- Cutting the wound, sucking out venom, tourniquets or ice.
- Waiting for signs to appear.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now.

Stay calm and focus on keeping him safe.

While it's happening:
- Move furniture and hard objects away. Only move him if he's near stairs, water or another danger.
- Keep your hands away from his mouth. He can't control his jaws and may bite without meaning to.
- Don't try to hold him down.
- Time the seizure, and take a short video for the vet if you can.

Go to your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic now if the seizure lasts more than about 3 minutes, if he has more than one in a row, or if he might have eaten something poisonous. Otherwise, call your vet soon after.

Afterward he may pace or seem confused. On the way to the vet, keep him calm, quiet and away from edges.

Yes. Please take him to a vet now, even if he looks fine. Some injuries don't show their full effects for a day or two, and pale gums, fast breathing or weakness can be signs of shock or internal bleeding.

To get him there safely:
- Be careful, because a hurt dog may bite. Use a cloth muzzle only if he is breathing normally and has no chest injury.
- If he can't walk well, slide him onto a firm, flat surface like a board or folded blanket, and keep his head, neck and back as still as possible.
- Keep him calm and quiet, and have someone else drive.

Call your vet or the nearest 24-hour clinic as you leave so they're ready for him.

Remove ticks as soon as you find them:

- Pull straight out with slow, steady pressure. Don't twist or jerk
- Don't use bare hands, matches, heat, nail polish or petroleum jelly
- Don't crush the tick. Drop it in rubbing alcohol, seal it in a bag or wrap it in tape
- Wash the bite area and your hands with soap and water

If small mouthparts stay in the skin, it usually heals on its own.
